cards.explanation: The assessment uses your observations and the supplied flowcharts for presumptive genus-level identification.
cards.text: The target taxonomic level for identifying the four unknown isolates is the {{c1::genus}}.
cards.question: The target taxonomic level for identifying the four unknown isolates is the {{c1::genus}}.

cards.explanation: A simplified teaching key narrows possibilities; it is not definitive clinical confirmation.
cards.text: The practical asks for {{c1::presumptive}} identifications using your own results and the supplied dichotomous keys.
cards.question: The practical asks for {{c1::presumptive}} identifications using your own results and the supplied dichotomous keys.

cards.explanation: No results for the four unknowns are supplied in this booklet, so their identities cannot be assigned in advance.
cards.text: For an unknown isolate, its identity must be inferred from {{c1::the observed practical results}}, rather than from its A–D label.
cards.question: For an unknown isolate, its identity must be inferred from {{c1::the observed practical results}}, rather than from its A–D label.

cards.explanation: The booklet describes preventing unwanted microorganisms from entering experimental cultures.
cards.text: Aseptic technique protects a culture from {{c1::environmental contamination}}.
cards.question: Aseptic technique protects a culture from {{c1::environmental contamination}}.

cards.explanation: The protection is two-way: avoiding culture contamination and protecting people and surroundings.
cards.text: Good microbiological practice also prevents laboratory cultures from {{c1::escaping into the environment}}.
cards.question: Good microbiological practice also prevents laboratory cultures from {{c1::escaping into the environment}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet states they can cause infectious disease. Follow the supervised laboratory rules.
cards.text: The microorganisms used in this practical are described as hazard category {{c1::2}}.
cards.question: The microorganisms used in this practical are described as hazard category {{c1::2}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet says to regard every microorganism as pathogenic for safe handling.
cards.text: An unknown microorganism should be treated as {{c1::potentially pathogenic}}.
cards.question: An unknown microorganism should be treated as {{c1::potentially pathogenic}}.

cards.explanation: Reducing unnecessary exposure limits opportunities for contamination.
cards.text: Cultures should be exposed to air for {{c1::no longer than necessary}}.
cards.question: Cultures should be exposed to air for {{c1::no longer than necessary}}.

cards.explanation: Contact with the bench can compromise the clean surface of the stopper.
cards.text: Tube caps should not be placed on the {{c1::bench}} during aseptic transfers.
cards.question: Tube caps should not be placed on the {{c1::bench}} during aseptic transfers.

cards.explanation: The booklet specifically lists aerosol avoidance among its microbiological safety rules.
cards.text: During microbiological handling, avoid producing {{c1::aerosols}}.
cards.question: During microbiological handling, avoid producing {{c1::aerosols}}.

cards.explanation: This avoids transferring unwanted organisms and leaving organisms on the used loop.
cards.text: The bacteriological loop is sterilised {{c1::before and after use}}.
cards.question: The bacteriological loop is sterilised {{c1::before and after use}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet requires reporting every accident; follow staff instructions for dealing with spills.
cards.text: Following a culture spill, the first reporting action is to {{c1::alert the demonstrator or lecturer immediately}}.
cards.question: Following a culture spill, the first reporting action is to {{c1::alert the demonstrator or lecturer immediately}}.
cards.answer: alert the demonstrator or lecturer immediately

cards.explanation: Use the laboratory’s approved pipetting equipment.
cards.text: Liquid must never be drawn into a pipette by {{c1::mouth}}.
cards.question: Liquid must never be drawn into a pipette by {{c1::mouth}}.

cards.explanation: The stated exit sequence is coat removal, handwashing and drying, then collecting personal items.
cards.text: A microbiology laboratory coat must be removed {{c1::before leaving the laboratory}}.
cards.question: A microbiology laboratory coat must be removed {{c1::before leaving the laboratory}}.

cards.explanation: The same person and the same digits are sampled on labelled halves of one plate.
cards.text: The handwashing plate compares fingertip growth {{c1::before and after washing}}.
cards.question: The handwashing plate compares fingertip growth {{c1::before and after washing}}.

cards.explanation: Changing the fingers sampled would introduce another explanation for a difference in growth.
cards.text: Using the same digits before and after washing helps keep the {{c1::sampling sites}} comparable.
cards.question: Using the same digits before and after washing helps keep the {{c1::sampling sites}} comparable.

cards.explanation: The method labels the base with the before/after division and the identifier.
cards.text: The two handwashing conditions are marked on the {{c1::base}} of the plate.
cards.question: The two handwashing conditions are marked on the {{c1::base}} of the plate.

cards.explanation: The booklet allows at least 10 minutes; its planning notes give an approximate 10–20-minute setting period.
cards.text: Before fingertips touch the handwashing plate, the poured agar must {{c1::set and dry}}.
cards.question: Before fingertips touch the handwashing plate, the poured agar must {{c1::set and dry}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet asks you to compare both abundance and types of growth, rather than only whether any growth occurred.
cards.text: The handwashing plate is assessed for the number and {{c1::variety of colonies}}.
cards.question: The handwashing plate is assessed for the number and {{c1::variety of colonies}}.

cards.explanation: This does not prove that all microorganisms were removed. The booklet supplies no actual before/after results.
cards.text: Fewer colonies after washing would support a reduction in {{c1::recoverable organisms under the test conditions}}.
cards.question: Fewer colonies after washing would support a reduction in {{c1::recoverable organisms under the test conditions}}.
cards.answer: recoverable organisms under the test conditions

cards.explanation: Do not assume washing produced a particular result when the plate data have not been supplied.
cards.text: A before/after handwashing conclusion must be based on {{c1::your observed colony results}}.
cards.question: A before/after handwashing conclusion must be based on {{c1::your observed colony results}}.

cards.explanation: The method specifies a cooled sterilised loop both for water transfer and for touching the colony.
cards.text: Before transferring cells for a Gram smear, the sterilised loop is allowed to {{c1::cool}}.
cards.question: Before transferring cells for a Gram smear, the sterilised loop is allowed to {{c1::cool}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet transfers a light touch of an isolated colony into the water on the slide.
cards.text: The colony used for the Gram smear should be {{c1::well isolated}}.
cards.question: The colony used for the Gram smear should be {{c1::well isolated}}.

cards.explanation: The procedure specifies a thin layer rather than a large clump of colony material.
cards.text: A Gram smear is spread as a {{c1::thin layer}} before drying.
cards.question: A Gram smear is spread as a {{c1::thin layer}} before drying.

cards.explanation: The source explicitly says not to hurry the drying artificially.
cards.text: A smear must {{c1::air dry}} before it is heat-fixed.
cards.question: A smear must {{c1::air dry}} before it is heat-fixed.

cards.explanation: The booklet passes the back of the slide through the blue Bunsen flame. Follow the demonstrated method.
cards.text: The step performed after air drying and before staining is {{c1::heat fixation}}.
cards.question: The step performed after air drying and before staining is {{c1::heat fixation}}.

cards.explanation: The protocol specifies 30 seconds before washing with distilled water.
cards.text: The primary stain in this Gram protocol is {{c1::methyl (crystal) violet}}.
cards.question: The primary stain in this Gram protocol is {{c1::methyl (crystal) violet}}.

cards.explanation: The iodine step lasts 30 seconds, followed by another distilled-water wash.
cards.text: The reagent applied after crystal violet and its water wash is {{c1::Lugol’s iodine}}.
cards.question: The reagent applied after crystal violet and its water wash is {{c1::Lugol’s iodine}}.

cards.explanation: It is applied after the iodine wash and is followed by a water wash. The booklet does not specify a decolourisation time.
cards.text: The decolourising reagent in this booklet is {{c1::alcohol/acetone}}.
cards.question: The decolourising reagent in this booklet is {{c1::alcohol/acetone}}.

cards.explanation: Use the reagent named in this booklet; do not substitute a different protocol’s counterstain. The source spells it “carbol fuschin”.
cards.text: The counterstain used in this practical is {{c1::carbol fuchsin}}.
cards.question: The counterstain used in this practical is {{c1::carbol fuchsin}}.

cards.explanation: Do not extend this timing to the alcohol/acetone step, whose duration is not specified.
cards.text: Crystal violet, iodine and carbol fuchsin are each applied for {{c1::30 seconds}} in this protocol.
cards.question: Crystal violet, iodine and carbol fuchsin are each applied for {{c1::30 seconds}} in this protocol.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. It helps form the crystal-violet–iodine complex. This explains why iodine follows the primary dye.
cards.text: Iodine acts as a {{c1::mordant}} in the Gram stain.
cards.question: Iodine acts as a {{c1::mordant}} in the Gram stain.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. Retention of the primary dye–iodine complex distinguishes the positive reaction.
cards.text: Correctly stained Gram-positive cells retain a {{c1::purple}} appearance.
cards.question: Correctly stained Gram-positive cells retain a {{c1::purple}} appearance.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. The counterstain colours cells that have lost the primary complex.
cards.text: After decolourisation and counterstaining, Gram-negative cells appear {{c1::pink/red}}.
cards.question: After decolourisation and counterstaining, Gram-negative cells appear {{c1::pink/red}}.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. Loss of the primary stain can mislead interpretation; the booklet does not specify a decolourisation duration.
cards.text: Excessive decolourisation can make Gram-positive cells appear falsely {{c1::Gram-negative}}.
cards.question: Excessive decolourisation can make Gram-positive cells appear falsely {{c1::Gram-negative}}.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. Residual primary stain can obscure the expected counterstained appearance.
cards.text: Insufficient decolourisation can make Gram-negative cells appear falsely {{c1::Gram-positive}}.
cards.question: Insufficient decolourisation can make Gram-negative cells appear falsely {{c1::Gram-positive}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet asks for cell colour and the shape of individual cells, checked while viewing.
cards.text: Microscopy records both Gram reaction and {{c1::cell shape}} for each isolate.
cards.question: Microscopy records both Gram reaction and {{c1::cell shape}} for each isolate.

cards.explanation: The full set consists of A–D on both agar types.
cards.text: Every unknown isolate must be streaked onto nutrient agar and {{c1::MacConkey agar}}.
cards.question: Every unknown isolate must be streaked onto nutrient agar and {{c1::MacConkey agar}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet asks whether isolated colonies were obtained; inadequate isolation may require repeating the step.
cards.text: The key target of purity streaking is {{c1::well-isolated individual colonies}}.
cards.question: The key target of purity streaking is {{c1::well-isolated individual colonies}}.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. This is the principle behind the purity-plating outcome requested by the booklet.
cards.text: Streaking progressively separates cells across the agar to obtain {{c1::isolated colonies}}.
cards.question: Streaking progressively separates cells across the agar to obtain {{c1::isolated colonies}}.

cards.explanation: The source specifies the NA plates for these primary identification tests, rather than the mixed original samples.
cards.text: Catalase and oxidase tests in week 2 use colonies from your {{c1::nutrient agar purity plates}}.
cards.question: Catalase and oxidase tests in week 2 use colonies from your {{c1::nutrient agar purity plates}}.

cards.explanation: Each pair needs A–D on NA plus A–D on MAC; each partner prepares four plates.
cards.text: A practical pair needs {{c1::eight}} purity plates to cover four isolates on two media.
cards.question: A practical pair needs {{c1::eight}} purity plates to cover four isolates on two media.

cards.explanation: The booklet names Oxoid CM0003 for NA and CM0007 for MAC, but does not reproduce their full formulations.
cards.text: The nutrient agar and MacConkey agar product information should be checked using the {{c1::manufacturer’s product codes}}.
cards.question: The nutrient agar and MacConkey agar product information should be checked using the {{c1::manufacturer’s product codes}}.

cards.explanation: Colony growth and lactose fermentation are separate observations; inspect the colour of colonies.
cards.text: The teaching key identifies lactose-fermenting growth on MacConkey by {{c1::pink colonies}}.
cards.question: The teaching key identifies lactose-fermenting growth on MacConkey by {{c1::pink colonies}}.

cards.explanation: A non-lactose-fermenter must first have grown. Follow the growth branch before the fermentation branch.
cards.text: No growth on MacConkey is different from {{c1::growth without lactose fermentation}}.
cards.question: No growth on MacConkey is different from {{c1::growth without lactose fermentation}}.

cards.explanation: This is a named teaching culture, not an identity assigned to any unknown A–D.
cards.text: The known isolate inoculated into urea broth is {{c1::Proteus spp.}}.
cards.question: The known isolate inoculated into urea broth is {{c1::Proteus spp.}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet pairs Proteus with UB and E. coli with NB.
cards.text: The known isolate inoculated into nutrient broth is {{c1::E. coli}}.
cards.question: The known isolate inoculated into nutrient broth is {{c1::E. coli}}.

cards.explanation: A baseline helps interpret the subsequent incubated culture.
cards.text: The appearance of each broth is recorded {{c1::before inoculation}}.
cards.question: The appearance of each broth is recorded {{c1::before inoculation}}.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. Turbidity alone is not a species identification or proof of purity; no actual broth observations are supplied.
cards.text: Increased turbidity of an inoculated nutrient broth is consistent with {{c1::microbial growth}}.
cards.question: Increased turbidity of an inoculated nutrient broth is consistent with {{c1::microbial growth}}.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. Ammonia production can make the medium more alkaline. The booklet does not name the urea-broth indicator or provide its colour chart.
cards.text: Urease catalyses the breakdown of {{c1::urea}}.
cards.question: Urease catalyses the breakdown of {{c1::urea}}.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. This links the biochemical reaction to an indicator response; use the actual supplied broth instructions for colour interpretation.
cards.text: Ammonia generated by urease tends to {{c1::raise the pH}} of the medium.
cards.question: Ammonia generated by urease tends to {{c1::raise the pH}} of the medium.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. The products are water and oxygen. The PDF names catalase as assessed but does not reproduce the test video’s detailed method.
cards.text: Catalase breaks down {{c1::hydrogen peroxide}}.
cards.question: Catalase breaks down {{c1::hydrogen peroxide}}.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. Interpret the reaction using the demonstrated assay. The booklet does not specify the reagent concentration or reading interval.
cards.text: Bubbling in a positive catalase reaction results from release of {{c1::oxygen}}.
cards.question: Bubbling in a positive catalase reaction results from release of {{c1::oxygen}}.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. The PDF names the test and supplies a video link, but does not give the exact reagent formulation, positive colour or reading time.
cards.text: The oxidase test is used to detect {{c1::cytochrome c oxidase}} activity.
cards.question: The oxidase test is used to detect {{c1::cytochrome c oxidase}} activity.

cards.explanation: It combines biochemical tests to help identify bacteria.
cards.text: API stands for {{c1::Analytical Profile Index}}.
cards.question: API stands for {{c1::Analytical Profile Index}}.

cards.explanation: The combined profile is compared with reference information; no single well gives the full identification.
cards.text: The API system identifies an isolate using a {{c1::profile of biochemical reactions}}.
cards.question: The API system identifies an isolate using a {{c1::profile of biochemical reactions}}.

cards.explanation: Use the named isolate provided for the strip; do not assume it is one of the four unknowns.
cards.text: The known organism used for the API strip in this practical is {{c1::E. coli}}.
cards.question: The known organism used for the API strip in this practical is {{c1::E. coli}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet specifies 9 mL for this suspension.
cards.text: The API inoculum is suspended in sterile {{c1::Ringer’s solution}}.
cards.question: The API inoculum is suspended in sterile {{c1::Ringer’s solution}}.

cards.explanation: The standard initial filling level is halfway; the boxed wells are the stated exception.
cards.text: API wells marked by three sides of a box are filled {{c1::to the top with the organism suspension}}.
cards.question: API wells marked by three sides of a box are filled {{c1::to the top with the organism suspension}}.
cards.answer: to the top with the organism suspension

cards.explanation: The method uses a second sterile pipette for the paraffin rather than the suspension pipette.
cards.text: Underlined API wells receive an overlay of sterile {{c1::liquid paraffin}}.
cards.question: Underlined API wells receive an overlay of sterile {{c1::liquid paraffin}}.

cards.explanation: The source distinguishes water in the chamber from the Ringer’s suspension used in wells.
cards.text: The API incubation chamber contains a few drops of {{c1::distilled water}}.
cards.question: The API incubation chamber contains a few drops of {{c1::distilled water}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet specifies one drop before reading the strip.
cards.text: The reagent added to the IND well is {{c1::James reagent}}.
cards.question: The reagent added to the IND well is {{c1::James reagent}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet specifies one drop.
cards.text: The reagent added to the TDA well is {{c1::TDA reagent}}.
cards.question: The reagent added to the TDA well is {{c1::TDA reagent}}.

cards.explanation: One drop of each reagent is added in the stated order.
cards.text: For the VP well, VP1 is added {{c1::before VP2}}.
cards.question: For the VP well, VP1 is added {{c1::before VP2}}.

cards.explanation: That chart is not reproduced in this PDF. Do not infer positive well colours from the protocol alone.
cards.text: API well colours are interpreted against the {{c1::provided colour chart}}.
cards.question: API well colours are interpreted against the {{c1::provided colour chart}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet does not reproduce the scoring worksheet, reaction weights or a completed profile.
cards.text: The biochemical reactions are scored to produce a {{c1::seven-digit}} identification number.
cards.question: The biochemical reactions are scored to produce a {{c1::seven-digit}} identification number.

cards.explanation: Do not choose a merely similar number when the booklet requires an exact match.
cards.text: An API identification number must be an {{c1::exact match}} in the supplied manual.
cards.question: An API identification number must be an {{c1::exact match}} in the supplied manual.

cards.explanation: The strip readings, colour chart and scoring worksheet are not supplied. No profile number has been invented.
cards.text: A full API profile cannot be calculated here without the {{c1::observed well reactions and scoring instructions}}.
cards.question: A full API profile cannot be calculated here without the {{c1::observed well reactions and scoring instructions}}.
cards.answer: observed well reactions and scoring instructions

cards.explanation: Work through lower magnifications before the final bacterial view.
cards.text: The stated objective sequence is ×4, ×10, ×40, then {{c1::×100}}.
cards.question: The stated objective sequence is ×4, ×10, ×40, then {{c1::×100}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet says not to lower the stage during lens changes and to rotate objectives using the collar.
cards.text: When changing objectives, refocus using the {{c1::fine control}}.
cards.question: When changing objectives, refocus using the {{c1::fine control}}.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. This is the standard oil-immersion objective referenced by the booklet’s microscopy question.
cards.text: The objective used with immersion oil in this practical is {{c1::×100}}.
cards.question: The objective used with immersion oil in this practical is {{c1::×100}}.

cards.explanation: Principle refresher: the booklet names this assessment topic but does not explain this mechanism in detail. This allows more light to enter the objective; it is a resolution aid, not extra magnification.
cards.text: Immersion oil improves resolution by reducing {{c1::refraction between the slide and objective}}.
cards.question: Immersion oil improves resolution by reducing {{c1::refraction between the slide and objective}}.
cards.answer: refraction between the slide and objective

cards.explanation: The booklet explicitly distinguishes lens tissue from blue tissue used to blot the stained slide.
cards.text: The ×100 lens is cleaned between slides with {{c1::lens tissue}}.
cards.question: The ×100 lens is cleaned between slides with {{c1::lens tissue}}.

cards.explanation: The booklet asks for staff confirmation at the microscope, rather than after viewing is finished.
cards.text: Gram reaction and cell shape should be checked {{c1::while the slide is still being viewed}}.
cards.question: Gram reaction and cell shape should be checked {{c1::while the slide is still being viewed}}.
cards.answer: while the slide is still being viewed

cards.explanation: Determine whether colonies are present before reading lactose fermentation. Within the booklet’s simplified 1994 teaching key; use as a presumptive practical interpretation, not a universal or definitive clinical identification.

cards.question: For Gram-negative rods, the first branch in the booklet’s key asks about {{c1::growth on MacConkey agar}}.

cards.text: Pink MacConkey colonies from a Gram-negative rod lead to {{c1::E. coli or Klebsiella spp.}} in the booklet’s key.
cards.question: Pink MacConkey colonies from a Gram-negative rod lead to {{c1::E. coli or Klebsiella spp.}} in the booklet’s key.

cards.question: The key separates E. coli from Klebsiella using additional {{c1::sugar tests}}.

cards.question: A Gram-negative rod with no MacConkey growth leads to a tentative {{c1::Haemophilus spp.}} suggestion in the booklet.

cards.question: After finding a non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod on MacConkey, the next test in the key is {{c1::oxidase}}.

cards.question: In the non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative Gram-negative rod branch, the next test is {{c1::urease}}.

cards.question: A non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative, urease-positive Gram-negative rod leads to {{c1::Proteus spp.}} in the key.

cards.question: For Gram-positive cocci, the first test in the booklet’s key is {{c1::catalase}}.

cards.question: Alpha-haemolytic, optochin-resistant organisms follow the key to the {{c1::viridans streptococci}} label.

cards.explanation: The source diagram separates sensitive and resistant branches at this point. Within the booklet’s simplified 1994 teaching key; use as a presumptive practical interpretation, not a universal or definitive clinical identification.

cards.question: The beta-haemolytic streptococcal branch is investigated with {{c1::bacitracin}}.

cards.explanation: Bacitracin susceptibility alone is not definitive species confirmation. Within the booklet’s simplified 1994 teaching key; use as a presumptive practical interpretation, not a universal or definitive clinical identification.
cards.text: Beta-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive streptococci lead to {{c1::S. pyogenes}} in the booklet’s diagram.
cards.question: Beta-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive streptococci lead to {{c1::S. pyogenes}} in the booklet’s diagram.

cards.explanation: The same note says most streptococci do not grow on this agar; “most” is not “all”. Within the booklet’s simplified 1994 teaching key; use as a presumptive practical interpretation, not a universal or definitive clinical identification.
cards.text: The key notes that {{c1::Enterococcus}} can grow on MacConkey despite its relation to streptococci.
cards.question: The key notes that {{c1::Enterococcus}} can grow on MacConkey despite its relation to streptococci.

cards.question: The Gram-negative, oxidase-positive coccal pathway is labelled {{c1::Neisseria spp.}}.

cards.question: In a binomial bacterial name, the {{c1::genus}} begins with a capital letter.

slides.text:
The target taxonomic level for identifying the four unknown isolates is the {{c1::genus}}.
For an unknown isolate, its identity must be inferred from {{c1::the observed practical results}}, rather than from its A–D label.
Urease catalyses the breakdown of {{c1::urea}}.
Ammonia generated by urease tends to {{c1::raise the pH}} of the medium.
Catalase breaks down {{c1::hydrogen peroxide}}.
Bubbling in a positive catalase reaction results from release of {{c1::oxygen}}.
The oxidase test is used to detect {{c1::cytochrome c oxidase}} activity.
In a binomial bacterial name, the {{c1::genus}} begins with a capital letter.
In a binomial bacterial name, the species epithet begins with a {{c1::lower-case letter}}.
“spp.” indicates {{c1::multiple species}} within a genus.
Liquid must never be drawn into a pipette by {{c1::mouth}}.

Aseptic technique protects a culture from {{c1::environmental contamination}}.
Good microbiological practice also prevents laboratory cultures from {{c1::escaping into the environment}}.
An unknown microorganism should be treated as {{c1::potentially pathogenic}}.
Cultures should be exposed to air for {{c1::no longer than necessary}}.
Tube caps should not be placed on the {{c1::bench}} during aseptic transfers.
During microbiological handling, avoid producing {{c1::aerosols}}.
The bacteriological loop is sterilised {{c1::before and after use}}.
Following a culture spill, the first reporting action is to {{c1::alert the demonstrator or lecturer immediately}}.
A microbiology laboratory coat must be removed {{c1::before leaving the laboratory}}.
The microorganisms used in this practical are described as hazard category {{c1::2}}.

The handwashing plate compares fingertip growth {{c1::before and after washing}}.
Using the same digits before and after washing helps keep the {{c1::sampling sites}} comparable.
The two handwashing conditions are marked on the {{c1::base}} of the plate.
Before fingertips touch the handwashing plate, the poured agar must {{c1::set and dry}}.

Before transferring cells for a Gram smear, the sterilised loop is allowed to {{c1::cool}}.
The colony used for the Gram smear should be {{c1::well isolated}}.
A Gram smear is spread as a {{c1::thin layer}} before drying.
A smear must {{c1::air dry}} before it is heat-fixed.
The step performed after air drying and before staining is {{c1::heat fixation}}.
The primary stain in this Gram protocol is {{c1::methyl (crystal) violet}}.
The reagent applied after crystal violet and its water wash is {{c1::Lugol’s iodine}}.
The decolourising reagent in this booklet is {{c1::alcohol/acetone}}.
The counterstain used in this practical is {{c1::carbol fuchsin}}.
Crystal violet, iodine and carbol fuchsin are each applied for {{c1::30 seconds}} in this protocol.
Iodine acts as a {{c1::mordant}} in the Gram stain.
Excessive decolourisation can make Gram-positive cells appear falsely {{c1::Gram-negative}}.
Insufficient decolourisation can make Gram-negative cells appear falsely {{c1::Gram-positive}}.
Every unknown isolate must be streaked onto nutrient agar and {{c1::MacConkey agar}}.
The ×100 lens is cleaned between slides with {{c1::lens tissue}}.

A practical pair needs {{c1::eight}} purity plates to cover four isolates on two media.
The nutrient agar and MacConkey agar product information should be checked using the {{c1::manufacturer’s product codes}}.
The known isolate inoculated into urea broth is {{c1::Proteus spp.}}.
The known isolate inoculated into nutrient broth is {{c1::E. coli}}.
The appearance of each broth is recorded {{c1::before inoculation}}.
API stands for {{c1::Analytical Profile Index}}.
The API system identifies an isolate using a {{c1::profile of biochemical reactions}}.
The known organism used for the API strip in this practical is {{c1::E. coli}}.

The API inoculum is suspended in sterile {{c1::Ringer’s solution}}.
API wells marked by three sides of a box are filled {{c1::to the top with the organism suspension}}.
Underlined API wells receive an overlay of sterile {{c1::liquid paraffin}}.
The API incubation chamber contains a few drops of {{c1::distilled water}}.
The reagent added to the IND well is {{c1::James reagent}}.
The reagent added to the TDA well is {{c1::TDA reagent}}.
For the VP well, VP1 is added {{c1::before VP2}}.
API well colours are interpreted against the {{c1::provided colour chart}}.
The biochemical reactions are scored to produce a {{c1::seven-digit}} identification number.
An API identification number must be an {{c1::exact match}} in the supplied manual.
A full API profile cannot be calculated here without the {{c1::observed well reactions and scoring instructions}}.

The handwashing plate is assessed for the number and {{c1::variety of colonies}}.
Fewer colonies after washing would support a reduction in {{c1::recoverable organisms under the test conditions}}.
A before/after handwashing conclusion must be based on {{c1::your observed colony results}}.
The key target of purity streaking is {{c1::well-isolated individual colonies}}.
Streaking progressively separates cells across the agar to obtain {{c1::isolated colonies}}.
Catalase and oxidase tests in week 2 use colonies from your {{c1::nutrient agar purity plates}}.
The stated objective sequence is ×4, ×10, ×40, then {{c1::×100}}.

The practical asks for {{c1::presumptive}} identifications using your own results and the supplied dichotomous keys.
Correctly stained Gram-positive cells retain a {{c1::purple}} appearance.
After decolourisation and counterstaining, Gram-negative cells appear {{c1::pink/red}}.
Microscopy records both Gram reaction and {{c1::cell shape}} for each isolate.
Increased turbidity of an inoculated nutrient broth is consistent with {{c1::microbial growth}}.
When changing objectives, refocus using the {{c1::fine control}}.
The objective used with immersion oil in this practical is {{c1::×100}}.
Immersion oil improves resolution by reducing {{c1::refraction between the slide and objective}}.
Gram reaction and cell shape should be checked {{c1::while the slide is still being viewed}}.

The teaching key identifies lactose-fermenting growth on MacConkey by {{c1::pink colonies}}.
No growth on MacConkey is different from {{c1::growth without lactose fermentation}}.
For Gram-negative rods, the first branch in the booklet’s key asks about {{c1::growth on MacConkey agar}}.
Pink MacConkey colonies from a Gram-negative rod lead to {{c1::E. coli or Klebsiella spp.}} in the booklet’s key.
The key separates E. coli from Klebsiella using additional {{c1::sugar tests}}.
A Gram-negative rod with no MacConkey growth leads to a tentative {{c1::Haemophilus spp.}} suggestion in the booklet.
After finding a non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod on MacConkey, the next test in the key is {{c1::oxidase}}.
A non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-positive Gram-negative rod follows the key to {{c1::Pseudomonas spp.}}.
In the non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative Gram-negative rod branch, the next test is {{c1::urease}}.
A non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative, urease-positive Gram-negative rod leads to {{c1::Proteus spp.}} in the key.
A non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-negative, urease-negative Gram-negative rod leads to {{c1::Salmonella spp. or Shigella spp.}} in the key.
The colony-spreading behaviour associated with Proteus in the key is {{c1::swarming on plain agar}}.
For Gram-positive cocci, the first test in the booklet’s key is {{c1::catalase}}.
Catalase-positive Gram-positive cocci lead to {{c1::Staphylococcus spp.}} in the key.
Catalase-negative Gram-positive cocci lead to {{c1::Streptococcus spp.}} in the key.
The next test used to subdivide Staphylococcus in the key is {{c1::coagulase}}.
The coagulase-positive Staphylococcus branch is labelled {{c1::S. aureus}}.
The coagulase-negative Staphylococcus branch is labelled {{c1::S. epidermidis}} in this key.
The streptococcal pathway is subdivided first by {{c1::haemolysis}}.
The alpha-haemolytic streptococcal branch is investigated with {{c1::optochin}} in the key.
Alpha-haemolytic, optochin-sensitive streptococci lead to {{c1::S. pneumoniae}} in the diagram.
Alpha-haemolytic, optochin-resistant organisms follow the key to the {{c1::viridans streptococci}} label.
The beta-haemolytic streptococcal branch is investigated with {{c1::bacitracin}}.
Beta-haemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive streptococci lead to {{c1::S. pyogenes}} in the booklet’s diagram.
The key notes that {{c1::Enterococcus}} can grow on MacConkey despite its relation to streptococci.
The Gram-negative, oxidase-positive coccal pathway is labelled {{c1::Neisseria spp.}}.
The Gram-positive rod example named in the key is {{c1::Bacillus spp.}}.
The key describes yeasts as large white colonies on {{c1::Sabouraud agar}}.
